data.kind: Results packet — blood tests and X-ray (12 days ago)
values: Periarticular osteopenia at MCPs; small marginal erosions right 2nd MCP and left 5th MTP; joint spaces preserved

script.opening: “Hi! I’m calling about my results. I looked on the app — the CCP one was negative, and I read that’s the main rheumatoid test, so that’s good, isn’t it?”

facts.text: “About ten weeks. Both hands, the knuckles — and the balls of my feet, like walking on pebbles. They’re puffy.”
“Every morning it takes over an hour before I can make a proper fist. Better once I get going.”
“I’m a hairdresser — I rent a chair, so if I don’t work I don’t get paid. I’ve dropped my scissors twice. Blow-drying kills my wrists. I’ve cut back to four days.”
“I’m tired all the time.” No fever, no weight loss, no rash, no mouth ulcers, no dry or red eyes, no psoriasis, no back pain, no recent diarrhoea or urine infection, no tick bite, no recent travel.

facts.topic: Painkillers (only if asked what you are taking)
facts.text: “Ibuprofen from the supermarket — two tablets, so 400, three times a day for about three weeks. It helps.”

facts.topic: Periods and pregnancy (only if asked about periods, contraception or pregnancy)
facts.text: Hesitate. “We stopped the pill three months ago — we’re trying for a baby. My period’s actually five days late. I haven’t done a test — I didn’t want to jinx it.”
“My nonna — my grandmother — had rheumatoid arthritis. Her hands were like claws. She couldn’t hold a cup by the end.” No psoriasis or lupus in the family.
Lives with partner Dan, a plumber. Non-smoker, never smoked. Alcohol: none since trying for a baby. Runs at weekends but stopped because of her feet.

Start upbeat — you think the negative test means you do not have RA. If the doctor explains it may still be RA, go quiet, then ask: “Will I end up like my nonna?” Only mention trying for a baby when periods, contraception or pregnancy come up — then become anxious: “Does this mean I can’t have a baby? I read the drugs for this cause birth defects.” If the doctor is clear and hopeful, settle and engage with the plan.

ice.ideas: “The anti-CCP was negative, so it’s probably not rheumatoid — maybe just overdoing it at work.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is trying to conceive and her period is late; she has been taking ibuprofen and fears that treatment for RA will mean giving up on a baby. Underneath is the image of her grandmother’s deformed hands and losing her livelihood.
ice.expectations: To be told the results are fine and get stronger painkillers so she can work.

cues: “The CCP one was negative, so that’s good, isn’t it?” — false reassurance to correct gently.
“If I don’t work I don’t get paid.” — financial pressure as a self-employed hairdresser.
“My nonna’s hands were like claws.” — the fear driving her denial.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the results correctly: weakly positive RF, negative anti-CCP, raised ESR and CRP, mild anaemia of inflammation, reactive thrombocytosis, early erosions on X-ray — probable early erosive rheumatoid arthritis; a negative anti-CCP does not exclude it

Updates the history: duration, distribution including feet, morning stiffness, function at work, systemic and extra-articular features, features of other inflammatory arthritides (psoriasis, IBD, recent infection, back pain)
Asks about medicines and about contraception, periods and pregnancy plans — finds she is trying to conceive, her period is late and she is taking regular ibuprofen
Refers urgently to rheumatology (to be seen within 3 weeks) and states the erosions, results and pregnancy plans in the referral; does not start steroids or DMARDs in primary care

Advises a pregnancy test today, stopping ibuprofen while trying to conceive and in pregnancy (paracetamol instead), and starting folic acid 400 micrograms daily; explains that rheumatology can choose pregnancy-compatible treatments and that methotrexate is avoided

Supports function and work: hand therapy and occupational therapy, joint protection, fit note or self-employed support options; safety-net for a hot swollen single joint with fever, new eye pain, or rapid worsening
Corrects the false reassurance about anti-CCP gently and honestly, and responds to the fear of her grandmother’s outcome with realistic hope about early treatment
Responds sensitively to the late period and pregnancy wish, involves her in decisions, and checks understanding

worked.lbl: Find out what she has read
worked.txt: “You’ve seen the results on the app — what did you make of them?”

“The CCP test is helpful when it’s positive, but about a third of people with rheumatoid arthritis have a negative one. The other tests — the inflammation markers and the X-ray — show your joints are inflamed and starting to be affected. So I think this is most likely early rheumatoid arthritis.”
“Your nonna would have been diagnosed at a time when treatment was very different. Now, starting the right medicines early — and you’re early — means most people keep their hands working well.”

worked.lbl: Ask the question that changes the plan
worked.txt: “Can I ask about your periods and contraception? Some of the treatments, and even the ibuprofen, matter if there’s any chance of pregnancy.”

“Please do a pregnancy test today. Stop the ibuprofen for now — it can make it harder to conceive and isn’t advised in pregnancy — and use paracetamol. Start folic acid. I’ll tell the rheumatologists you’re trying for a baby; there are treatments that are safe in pregnancy.”
“I’m referring you urgently — you should be seen within about three weeks. If one joint becomes hot, very swollen and you feel feverish, contact us the same day.”

f.learning: In suspected inflammatory arthritis, serology is supportive, not decisive: around a third of people with rheumatoid arthritis are seronegative, and early erosions with raised inflammatory markers and clinical synovitis of the small joints make the diagnosis probable whatever the anti-CCP shows. NICE NG100 recommends urgent referral for persistent synovitis of unknown cause, especially if the small joints of the hands or feet or more than one joint are affected, and the quality standard is assessment within 3 weeks of referral — erosions at ten weeks make this even more pressing. The GP role is not to start disease-modifying treatment but to refer quickly, give honest information, manage symptoms safely and spot what will change specialist decisions. Here the key question is about pregnancy: NSAIDs may reduce fertility and are generally avoided in pregnancy, methotrexate and leflunomide are teratogenic, while hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and some biologics are compatible with conception and pregnancy. Telling her that a pregnancy plan is part of rheumatology care — not an obstacle to it — turns fear into a plan.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG100 Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management (2018, updated 2020) · NICE QS33 Rheumatoid arthritis in over 16s (2013, updated 2020) · British Society for Rheumatology guideline on prescribing drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding (2022) · NICE NG201 Antenatal care (2021)
knowledge.summary: Erosions plus raised ESR and CRP with small-joint synovitis = probable early RA despite a negative anti-CCP: urgent rheumatology referral, pregnancy test, stop ibuprofen, folic acid, and a treatment plan built around her wish for a baby.

points.t: Rheumatoid factor: sensitivity about 70%, also positive in other conditions and some healthy people. Anti-CCP: highly specific, predicts erosive disease, but negative in roughly a third. ESR and CRP reflect activity. Normocytic anaemia and raised platelets are typical of active inflammation. Early X-ray signs: periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions at MCP and MTP joints.

NICE NG100: refer urgently for persistent synovitis of unknown cause; urgency increases if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or more since symptom onset. Do not withhold referral because RF or anti-CCP is negative. QS33: seen within 3 weeks of referral.

Analgesia and short-term NSAIDs can be used if appropriate; glucocorticoids are usually started by the specialist. In someone trying to conceive, avoid NSAIDs (possible reversible effect on ovulation; avoid in pregnancy, particularly from 20 weeks) and use paracetamol.

BSR 2022: hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine (with folic acid 5 mg daily, specialist advice) are compatible with pregnancy; TNF inhibitors can be continued in pregnancy in many cases; methotrexate must be stopped 1 month before conception in women (no routine stop for men on ≤25 mg/week) and leflunomide needs a washout. Pre-conception counselling is part of rheumatology care.

All women trying to conceive: folic acid 400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks of pregnancy (NICE NG201). Usual adult dose as stated (check the SPC, BNF and local formulary; SPC: folic acid 400 microgram tablets). Higher doses may be advised by the specialist with sulfasalazine.
Hand therapy and occupational therapy for joint protection, splints and adapted tools; self-employed people can receive a fit note to support claims; Access to Work can fund equipment.
The Clear pass candidate corrects the negative-test misunderstanding without crushing hope, asks the pregnancy question, and writes the pregnancy plan into the referral.

model.text: Hi Sofia, it’s Dr Begum. Can you see and hear me OK? You’ve had a look at your results — what did you make of them?
The CCP one was negative — I read that’s the main rheumatoid test, so that’s good, isn’t it?
I can see why you’d think that. Before I go through them, can I check how your hands and feet are now?
model.why: Holds the explanation until the history is updated

model.text: Same. Puffy knuckles, over an hour to loosen up in the morning, and my feet feel like pebbles.
How is it affecting work and home? Any tiredness, fever, rashes, dry or red eyes, psoriasis, bowel problems or back pain?
model.why: Function plus systemic and other inflammatory arthritis features

model.text: I’ve dropped my scissors and cut down to four days — I’m self-employed. Tired. None of the others.
What are you taking for the pain? And can I ask about periods and contraception — it affects which treatments are safe.
model.why: Medicines and the pregnancy question, with a reason

model.text: Ibuprofen, 400 three times a day. We stopped the pill three months ago — we’re trying. My period’s five days late.

Thank you for telling me — that’s really important. About the results: the CCP test is useful when it’s positive, but about a third of people with rheumatoid arthritis have a negative one. Your inflammation markers are high, and the X-ray shows early changes in two joints. Putting it together, I think this is most likely early rheumatoid arthritis.
Will I end up like my nonna? Her hands were like claws.
That must have been hard to watch. Treatment now is very different — starting early, which is where you are, means most people keep their hands working well. That’s why I want you seen quickly.
model.why: Responds to the fear with realistic hope

model.text: I’m referring you urgently to rheumatology — usually seen within three weeks. Today, please do a pregnancy test, stop the ibuprofen and use paracetamol, and start folic acid 400 micrograms a day.
model.why: Urgent referral and pregnancy-safe interim plan

model.text: Does this mean I can’t have a baby? I read the drugs cause birth defects.

No. Some medicines, like methotrexate, aren’t used when trying for a baby, but others are safe in pregnancy. I’ll put in the letter that you’re trying to conceive so they plan around it. I’ll also refer you to hand therapy and an occupational therapist for work.
model.why: Accurate reassurance; pregnancy plan in the referral; function

model.text: If one joint becomes hot and very swollen with a fever, or the pain suddenly gets much worse, contact us the same day. Let me know the pregnancy test result. What will you do when we finish?
Pregnancy test, stop ibuprofen, paracetamol, folic acid — and wait for the rheumatology letter. And you’ll tell them about the baby.

social.t: A chair-renting hairdresser has no sick pay; reduced grip directly reduces income. Ask, and offer fit notes, OT and benefits signposting.
A relative’s severe disability often shapes how people hear a diagnosis. Naming it and contrasting modern care helps engagement.

legal.t: Patients increasingly see results before the clinician explains them; ask what they have read before explaining.

professional.t: A good referral includes the results, erosions, duration, and the pregnancy plan, so the rheumatologist can choose treatment at the first visit.

professional.h: Prescribing safely in women of child-bearing potential
professional.t: Ask about contraception and pregnancy plans before advising NSAIDs or teratogenic drugs.

community.t: National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) information on RA and pregnancy; Versus Arthritis; Access to Work for workplace adaptations.

redFlags: Hot, swollen single joint with fever (septic arthritis)
Systemic features — fever, weight loss, rash (consider connective tissue disease)
ice: Idea: negative test means no RA
Concern: baby; hands like her nonna’s
core: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day

playbook.diagnosis: Probable early rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory, erosive, RF weakly positive, anti-CCP negative), in a woman trying to conceive with a late period on regular NSAIDs.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your joints are inflamed and starting to be affected — most likely early rheumatoid arthritis. The negative test doesn’t rule it out. The good news is we’ve caught it early.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped the negative test meant this wasn’t rheumatoid, and you’re worried about having a baby and about your nonna’s hands. Early treatment protects your hands, and the specialists can plan treatment that works with a pregnancy.”
management.psychosocial: OT and hand therapy for work; fit note if needed; Dan involved if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Urgent rheumatology referral (within 3 weeks), including pregnancy plans
safetyNet: Hot swollen single joint with fever — same day
New red painful eye or rapid worsening — call
Positive pregnancy test — tell us and book antenatal care

pitfalls.intro: A results station with a trap in the patient’s first sentence and a second trap she does not volunteer.

items.fail: Agrees that a negative anti-CCP is reassuring, or reads the X-ray as “mild wear and tear”.
items.why: Seronegative RA is common; early erosions mean active, damaging disease.
items.fix: Interpret the whole packet with the clinical picture: synovitis, morning stiffness, inflammatory markers, erosions.

items.fail: Recommends a stronger NSAID (or naproxen with a PPI) without asking about pregnancy.
items.why: She may be pregnant and is trying to conceive; NSAIDs may reduce fertility and are avoided in pregnancy.
items.fix: Ask about contraception and periods before prescribing; pregnancy test; paracetamol meanwhile.

items.fail: Says “You’ll need methotrexate, so you’ll have to put the baby on hold.”
items.why: Inaccurate and devastating; treatment choices are made by the specialist around her plans.
items.fix: Explain that pregnancy-compatible options exist and that you will tell rheumatology.

timeMap.d: Ask what she made of the results.
Joints, stiffness, function, systemic features; medicines; periods and pregnancy.
Negative anti-CCP does not exclude RA; erosions and inflammation; respond to nonna fear.
Urgent referral with pregnancy plan; pregnancy test; stop NSAID; folic acid; hand therapy and OT.

wordPics.clearFail: Reassures that the negative anti-CCP rules out RA, advises more ibuprofen or naproxen, no urgent referral, never asks about pregnancy.
wordPics.fail: Refers to rheumatology but routinely, or gives NSAID advice without a pregnancy question, or leaves her believing treatment means no baby.
wordPics.pass: Interprets the results correctly; urgent referral; finds the pregnancy plan; pregnancy test, stop NSAID, folic acid; mentions pregnancy-compatible treatment; safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass with real warmth: starts from what she read online, corrects it gently, contrasts her nonna’s era with early treatment today, writes the pregnancy plan into the referral, addresses her income, and closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “The main test was negative, so it’s probably not rheumatoid.”
avoid.instead: “A negative CCP doesn’t rule it out — the other results and the X-ray point towards early rheumatoid arthritis.”

avoid.dont: “Take naproxen twice a day with omeprazole.”
avoid.instead: “Before I suggest anything stronger — is there any chance you could be pregnant?”

avoid.dont: “These drugs aren’t safe in pregnancy, so you’ll have to wait.”
avoid.instead: “Some treatments are safe in pregnancy — the rheumatologists will plan around you.”
